summary.text: For $p\equiv3\pmod4$, quadratic-character sums give commuting difference/sum matrices $N,P$ with $(N+P)(N+P)^T=pI-2E$; after a column permutation the target is $\tfrac12(S-S^TZ)$ for a symmetric involution $Z$ of determinant $1$, and an odd-dimensional orthogonal-matrix argument makes this singular. For $p\equiv1\pmod4$, reduction modulo $p$ and Euler’s criterion turn a hypothetical kernel vector into moment equations; Vandermonde inversion and the polynomial $\prod_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2}(X-k)$ force all moments to vanish, using Wilson’s theorem for $((p-1)/2)!^2=-1$ to exclude the remaining exceptional factor, so the reduced determinant is nonzero.

full_proof.text:
Let \(p\) be an odd prime and put
\[
 m=\frac{p-1}{2}=\left\lfloor\frac p2\right\rfloor,
 \qquad C=m!.
\]
Write \(\mathbf F_p\) for the field with \(p\) elements and write
\(\chi:\mathbf F_p\to\{-1,0,1\}\) for its quadratic character, extended by
\(\chi(0)=0\). For \(1\le i,j\le m\), define
\[
 \rho_i=i^2\in\mathbf F_p,
 \qquad w_j=Cj\in\mathbf F_p,
 \qquad A_{ij}=\chi(\rho_i-w_j)=\chi(i^2-Cj).
\]
The determinant in the sequence is precisely \(\det A\), where the entries are regarded as integers. We prove
\[
 \det A=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\equiv3\pmod4.
\]
Afterward we apply this to the \(n\)-th prime.


1. A quadratic character-sum formula
-----------------------------------

We will repeatedly use the following standard formula. If \(K\) is a finite field of odd cardinality \(q\), with quadratic character \(\chi_K\), then for \(\beta,\gamma\in K\),
\[
 \sum_{x\in K}\chi_K(x^2+\beta x+\gamma)
 =
 \begin{cases}
 q-1,&\beta^2-4\gamma=0,\\
 -1,&\beta^2-4\gamma\ne0.
 \end{cases}                                      \tag{1}
\]
Here is a proof, included for completeness. First,
\[
 \sum_{x\in K}\chi_K(x^2)=q-1,
\]
because the term at \(x=0\) is zero and every other term is one. More generally, for \(\delta\ne0\), count the pairs \((x,y)\in K^2\) satisfying
\[
 y^2=x^2+\delta.
\]
For each fixed \(x\), the number of possible \(y\)'s is
\(1+\chi_K(x^2+\delta)\). On the other hand, since the characteristic is not two, the invertible change of variables
\[
 (x,y)\longmapsto (u,v)=(y-x,y+x)

a identifies these pairs with solutions of \(uv=\delta\). There are exactly \(q-1\) such solutions: choose any \(u\ne0\), and then \(v=\delta/u\). Consequently
\[
 q+\sum_x\chi_K(x^2+\delta)=q-1,
\]
so the character sum is \(-1\). Finally, completing the square gives
\[
 x^2+\beta x+\gamma
 =\left(x+\frac\beta2\right)^2+ rac{4\gamma-\beta^2}{4}.
\]
Translation by \(\beta/2\) permutes the field, and the last constant is zero exactly when the discriminant \(\beta^2-4\gamma\) is zero. This proves (1).


2. Nonsingularity when \(p\equiv1\pmod4\)
------------------------------------------

Assume first that \(p\equiv1\pmod4\). Thus \(p=2m+1\), \(m\) is even, and in fact \(p\ge5\). Let
\[
 F=C=m!\in\mathbf F_p.
\]
None of \(1,2,\ldots,m\), and hence neither \(F\), vanishes in \(\mathbf F_p\).

Consider the matrix over \(\mathbf F_p\)
\[
 B_{ij}=(i^2-Fj)^m,\qquad 1\le i,j\le m.             \tag{2}
\]
We prove that \(B\) is nonsingular.

First note two elementary facts. The elements
\[
 1^2,2^2,\ldots,m^2
\]
are pairwise distinct in \(\mathbf F_p\). Indeed, if \(i^2=j^2\), then
\((i-j)(i+j)=0\). Either \(i=j\), or \(i+j=p\); the second alternative is impossible because \(2\le i+j\le2m=p-1\). Also, by Fermat's theorem,
\[
 (i^2)^m=i^{2m}=i^{p-1}=1.                          \tag{3}
\]

We also need the value of \(F^2\). Wilson's theorem says
\((p-1)!=-1\) in \(\mathbf F_p\). Pair the factors in the upper half with negatives of the factors in the lower half:
\[
 (p-1)!=1\cdots m\,(m+1)\cdots(2m)=(-1)^m(m!)^2.
\]
Since \(m\) is even, this yields
\[
 F^2=-1.                                             \tag{4}
\]
In particular \(F\ne1\) and \(F\ne-1\), since an odd-characteristic field has \(1\ne-1\). If \(m=2k\), then
\[
 F^{m+1}=F^{2k+1}=(-1)^kF\ne1.                      \tag{5}
\]

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(B\) is singular. Choose a nonzero vector
\(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\in\mathbf F_p^m\) with \(Bv=0\). Define its moments
\[
 \mu_r=\sum_{j=1}^m v_jj^r\qquad(r\ge0),            \tag{6}
\]
and, for \(0\le t\le m\), define
\[
 a_t=\binom mt(-F)^{m-t}\mu_{m-t}.                  \tag{7}
\]
Expanding each row equation by the binomial theorem gives, for every
\(i=1,\ldots,m\),
\[
 0=\sum_{j=1}^m(i^2-Fj)^m v_j
   =\sum_{t=0}^m(i^2)^t a_t.                        \tag{8}
\]
Since \(a_m=\mu_0\), equation (3) reduces this to
\[
 \sum_{t=0}^{m-1}(i^2)^t a_t=-\mu_0.                \tag{9}
\]

The Vandermonde matrix on the distinct nodes \(1^2,\ldots,m^2\), with powers
\(0,\ldots,m-1\), is invertible. Thus the only polynomial of degree at most
\(m-1\) vanishing at all these nodes is the zero polynomial. Applying this to
\[
 a_0+\mu_0+a_1X+\cdots+a_{m-1}X^{m-1},
\]
which vanishes at all the nodes by (9), gives
\[
 a_0=-\mu_0,
 \qquad a_t=0\quad(1\le t<m).                       \tag{10}
\]
For \(1\le r<m\), take \(t=m-r\) in (7). The binomial coefficient
\(\binom m{m-r}\) is nonzero in \(\mathbf F_p\): indeed, all factorials involved have arguments less than \(p\), so none is divisible by \(p\). Also \(F\ne0\). Hence (10) implies
\[
 \mu_r=0\qquad(1\le r<m).                           \tag{11}
\]
The equation for \(a_0\) gives
\[
 (-F)^m\mu_m=-\mu_0.
\]
Because \(m\) is even, this is
\[
 F^m\mu_m=-\mu_0.                                  \tag{12}
\]

We now obtain a second relation between \(\mu_m\) and \(\mu_0\). Let
\[
 g(X)=\prod_{j=1}^m(X-j)
     =\sum_{r=0}^m c_rX^r\in\mathbf F_p[X].
\]
This is monic, so \(c_m=1\), and its constant term is
\[
 c_0=(-1)^m m!=F,                                   \tag{13}
\]
again because \(m\) is even. Since \(g(j)=0\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,m\),
\[
 0=\sum_{j=1}^m v_jg(j)
  =\sum_{r=0}^m c_r\mu_r.
\]
All intermediate moments vanish by (11), and therefore, using (13),
\[
 \mu_m=-F\mu_0.                                     \tag{14}
\]
Combining (12) and (14) gives
\[
 (F^{m+1}-1)\mu_0=0.
\]
By (5), \(F^{m+1}-1\ne0\), so \(\mu_0=0\). Equations (11) now show
\[
 \mu_r=0\qquad(0\le r<m).
\]
But the Vandermonde matrix on the distinct nodes \(1,2,\ldots,m\) is invertible. The equations
\(\sum_jv_jj^r=0\) for \(0\le r<m\) therefore imply \(v=0\), contradicting our choice. Hence \(B\) is nonsingular.

Euler's criterion states that for every \(x\in\mathbf F_p\), including \(x=0\),
\[
 \chi(x)=x^{(p-1)/2}=x^m.
\]
Thus reducing every integer entry of \(A\) modulo \(p\) gives precisely the matrix \(B\) in (2). If the integer determinant \(\det A\) were zero, its reduction modulo \(p\) would also be zero, contrary to the nonsingularity of \(B\). We conclude that
\[
 p\equiv1\pmod4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\det A\ne0. \tag{15}
\]


3. Singularity when \(p\equiv3\pmod4\)
---------------------------------------

Now assume \(p\equiv3\pmod4\). Then \(p=2m+1\) with \(m\) odd, and
\[
 \chi(-1)=-1.                                       \tag{16}
\]
The nonzero squares in \(\mathbf F_p\) are exactly
\[
 \rho_i=i^2,\qquad1\le i\le m.
\]
Indeed, these \(m\) elements are nonzero and distinct by the same elementary argument used above. Because of (16), no \(\rho_i\) is the negative of a \(\rho_j\). Consequently
\[
 \{\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_m,-\rho_1,\ldots,-\rho_m\}
   =\mathbf F_p^\times.                              \tag{17}
\]
It follows that, for every function \(f:\mathbf F_p\to\mathbf Z\),
\[
 \sum_{k=1}^m f(\rho_k)+\sum_{k=1}^m f(-\rho_k)
 =\sum_{u\in\mathbf F_p}f(u)-f(0).                  \tag{18}
\]

Define integer matrices \(N,P\) by
\[
 N_{ij}=\chi(\rho_i-\rho_j),
 \qquad P_{ij}=\chi(\rho_i+\rho_j).                 \tag{19}
\]
We next establish the identities
\[
 N^2-P^2=2E-pI,                                     \tag{20}
\]
\[
 NP=PN,                                             \tag{21}
\]
where \(E\) denotes the all-ones matrix.

Fix \(i,j\), and set
\[
 f(u)=\chi(\rho_i-u)\chi(u-\rho_j).
\]
The \((i,j)\)-entry of \(N^2\) is \(\sum_k f(\rho_k)\). Moreover, by multiplicativity of \(\chi\) and (16),
\[
 P_{ik}P_{kj}=-f(-\rho_k).
\]
Thus (18) gives
\[
 (N^2-P^2)_{ij}=\sum_{u\in\mathbf F_p}f(u)-f(0).    \tag{22}
\]
Now
\[
 f(u)=-\chi\bigl(u^2-(\rho_i+\rho_j)u+\rho_i\rho_j\bigr).

aThe discriminant of the quadratic inside the character is
\((\rho_i-\rho_j)^2\), which is zero exactly when \(i=j\). Formula (1) therefore shows
\[
 \sum_uf(u)=
 \begin{cases}
 1-p,&i=j,\\
 1,&i\ne j.
 \end{cases}

aAlso
\[
 f(0)=\chi(\rho_i)\chi(-\rho_j)=-1.
\]
Substitution in (22) gives \(2-p\) on the diagonal and \(2\) off the diagonal, which is exactly (20).

For (21), set instead
\[
 h(u)=\chi(\rho_i-u)\chi(u+\rho_j).
\]
As above,
\[
 (NP-PN)_{ij}=\sum_{u\in\mathbf F_p}h(u)-h(0).       \tag{23}
\]
We have
\[
 h(u)=-\chi\bigl(u^2+(\rho_j-\rho_i)u-\rho_i\rho_j\bigr).
\]
Its discriminant is \((\rho_i+\rho_j)^2\), which is nonzero: otherwise \(\rho_i=-\rho_j\), impossible by (16). Formula (1) gives \(\sum_uh(u)=1\), while
\(h(0)=\chi(\rho_i)\chi(\rho_j)=1\). Hence (23) is zero, proving (21).

We also have
\[
 N^T=-N,
 \qquad P^T=P.                                      \tag{24}
\]
The second identity is immediate. For the first,
\[
 \chi(\rho_j-\rho_i)=\chi(-1)\chi(\rho_i-\rho_j)
 =-\chi(\rho_i-\rho_j).
\]

Regard these matrices now as rational matrices and put
\[
 S=N+P.
\]
Using (21) and (24),
\[
 SS^T=(N+P)(P-N)=-(N^2-P^2)=pI-2E,                 \tag{25}
\]
and similarly
\[
 S^TS=pI-2E.                                        \tag{26}
\]
Thus \(S\) is normal: \(SS^T=S^TS\).

Moreover, \(S\) is invertible. It suffices by (25) to show that \(pI-2E\) has trivial kernel. If
\((pI-2E)v=0\), and \(T=\sum_jv_j\), then every coordinate satisfies
\[
 pv_i=2T.
\]
Summing over \(i\) gives
\[
 pT=2mT.
\]
Since \(p=2m+1\), this forces \(T=0\), and then \(pv_i=0\) forces every \(v_i=0\). Therefore \(SS^T\), and hence \(S\), is invertible.

We now relate \(S\) to the desired matrix \(A\). Each \(w_j=Cj\) is nonzero, because \(C=m!\) and \(j\) are nonzero modulo \(p\). Exactly one of \(w_j\) and \(-w_j\) is a square, by (16). Let
\[
 q_j=
 \begin{cases}
 w_j,&\chi(w_j)=1,\\
 -w_j,&\chi(w_j)=-1.
 \end{cases}

aThen \(q_j\) is a nonzero square, so there is an index \(\sigma(j)\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) such that
\[
 \rho_{\sigma(j)}=q_j.                              \tag{27}
\]
The map \(\sigma\) is a permutation. Indeed,
\[
 q_j^2=w_j^2=C^2j^2=C^2\rho_j.
\]
If \(q_j=q_{j'}\), cancellation of the nonzero \(C^2\) gives
\(\rho_j=\rho_{j'}\), and hence \(j=j'\). Thus \(\sigma\) is injective on a finite set of size \(m\), so it is bijective.

Equation (27) gives the following column description of \(A\):
\[
 A_{ij}=
 \begin{cases}
 N_{i,\sigma(j)},&\chi(w_j)=1,\\
 P_{i,\sigma(j)},&\chi(w_j)=-1.
 \end{cases}                                        \tag{28}
\]
Indeed, in the first case \(\rho_{\sigma(j)}=w_j\), and in the second case
\(\rho_{\sigma(j)}=-w_j\).

Define a diagonal rational matrix \(Z\), indexed after the permutation \(\sigma\), by
\[
 Z_{kk}=\eta_k,
 \qquad \eta_{\sigma(j)}=\chi(w_j).
\]
Every diagonal entry is \(\pm1\), so
\[
 Z^T=Z,
 \qquad Z^2=I.                                      \tag{29}
\]
We also claim
\[
 \det Z=1.                                          \tag{30}
\]
Since permutation does not alter a product,
\[
 \det Z=\prod_{j=1}^m\chi(w_j)
       =\chi\left(\prod_{j=1}^m w_j\right).
\]
But
\[
 \prod_{j=1}^m w_j
 =\prod_{j=1}^m(Cj)=C^m m!=C^{m+1}.
\]
Because \(m\) is odd, \(m+1\) is even, and therefore
\[
 \chi(C^{m+1})=\chi(C)^{m+1}=1.
\]
This proves (30).

We need one elementary odd-dimensional linear-algebra fact.

**Lemma.** Let \(r\) be odd. Suppose \(S\) is an invertible rational
\(r\times r\) matrix satisfying \(SS^T=S^TS\), and suppose \(Z\) satisfies
\[
 Z^T=Z,\qquad Z^2=I,\qquad\det Z=1.
\]
Then
\[
 \det(S-S^TZ)=0.                                    \tag{31}
\]

To prove the lemma, define
\[
 O=S^{-1}S^TZ.
\]
Normality of \(S\), together with the displayed properties of \(Z\), gives
\[
 O^TO=I.
\]
For clarity, one may compute
\[
 O^T=ZS(S^T)^{-1},

aand use the consequence
\((S^T)^{-1}S^{-1}=S^{-1}(S^T)^{-1}\) of
\(SS^T=S^TS\); all adjacent inverse factors then cancel and leave \(Z^2=I\).
Also
\[
 \det O=\det(S^{-1})\det(S^T)\det Z=1.
\]
For any odd-dimensional orthogonal matrix with determinant one,
\(\det(I-O)=0\). Indeed, orthogonality gives \(OO^T=I\), and
\[
 O-I=O(I-O^T).
\]
Taking determinants and using \(\det O=1\) and
\(\det(I-O^T)=\det(I-O)\) yields
\[
 \det(O-I)=\det(I-O).
\]
On the other hand, because the dimension is odd,
\[
 \det(O-I)=\det(-(I-O))=-\det(I-O).
\]
Hence \(\det(I-O)=0\). Finally,
\[
 S-S^TZ=S(I-O),
\]
which proves (31).

Apply the lemma to our \(S\) and \(Z\); its hypotheses follow from
(25), (26), (29), and (30). Thus
\[
 \det(S-S^TZ)=0.                                    \tag{32}
\]
Now inspect the \((i,\sigma(j))\)-entry of
\(\frac12(S-S^TZ)\). Since \(N^T=-N\) and \(P^T=P\), it equals
\[
 \frac12\bigl((N_{i,\sigma(j)}+P_{i,\sigma(j)})
 -(-N_{i,\sigma(j)}+P_{i,\sigma(j)})\chi(w_j)\bigr).
\]
If \(\chi(w_j)=1\), this is \(N_{i,\sigma(j)}\); if
\(\chi(w_j)=-1\), it is \(P_{i,\sigma(j)}\). By (28), after permuting columns by \(\sigma\), the matrix \(\frac12(S-S^TZ)\) is exactly \(A\), regarded as a rational matrix. Equation (32) therefore implies
\[
 \det A=0.

aSince the entries and determinant of \(A\) are integers, vanishing over the rationals is the same as vanishing as an integer. We have proved
\[
 p\equiv3\pmod4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\det A=0.  \tag{33}
\]
Together, (15) and (33) establish the desired equivalence for every odd prime \(p\).


4. Identification with the OEIS sequence
-----------------------------------------

For \(n\ge2\), let \(p=p_n\) be the \(n\)-th prime. Since \(n\ge2\), this is not \(2\), hence it is odd. Therefore
\[
 \frac{p-1}{2}=\left\lfloor\frac p2\right\rfloor=m.
\]
The sequence term \(a(n)\) is the determinant of the \(m\times m\) matrix whose \((i,j)\)-entry, for \(1\le i,j\le m\), is the Legendre symbol
\[
 \left(\frac{i^2-m!\,j}{p}\right).
\]
For a prime denominator, this Legendre symbol is exactly the quadratic character of the residue class of its numerator in \(\mathbf F_p\). Thus this matrix is precisely the integer matrix \(A\) used above. We conclude
\[
 a(n)=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p_n\equiv3\pmod4,

afor every \(n\ge2\), as claimed.
